title: Choose the regional dishes your guests will recognise and enjoy
focus: Start with the culinary direction: a North Indian celebration, South Indian meal or a selection of family favourites. Balance rice, breads, vegetables, pulses and main dishes so each part has a purpose. A live dosa, tandoor or chaat station can add interest when the venue and programme support it. Discuss spice preferences dish by dish and confirm Jain or other observances precisely. The final menu should bring regional character and thoughtful service together, without overwhelming guests with too many choices.

sections.title: Choose a regional direction before expanding the selection
paragraphs: Choose the kind of Indian meal you want before expanding the dish list: a North Indian celebration, a South Indian direction, a chaat-led reception or a mixed regional buffet. Use a few favourite dishes to describe the occasion rather than asking for every regional style at once.

Tell us the vegetarian and non-vegetarian guest counts and the spice preferences of adults and children. Specify ingredients to avoid and any Jain or other dietary requirements so the proposed menu can be reviewed dish by dish.

Think about how starters, breads, rice and mains will be served together. A live station needs an agreed working area and service plan; a delivered meal needs a clear handover and someone to serve it. Ask for those differences to be itemised before choosing the format.

sections.title: Give the menu a clear direction
paragraphs: Begin with a few dishes or flavours that your guests will enjoy, then build a balanced selection around them. A strong menu includes variety in texture, colour and richness without trying to cover every possible preference with a separate dish. The most useful question is how the food will work as a complete meal or reception.

Consider the time of day and the length of service. A short welcome reception needs a different amount and style of food from an evening where canapés replace dinner. Similarly, a working lunch should be easy to serve and enjoy within the available break.

Menu examples are a starting point for discussion. Ingredients, dietary variations and the practical requirements of your venue need to be reviewed before the final selection is confirmed. That gives the team room to recommend food that suits the occasion and can be served well.

sections.title: Make plant-based food a complete experience
paragraphs: A plant-based menu should offer substance, contrast and variety. Consider a combination of vegetables, grains, legumes and sauces, with textures that make the meal satisfying from the first course to the last. The aim is a selection guests will enjoy for its flavour and balance.

Be precise about the brief. Vegetarian, vegan and dairy-free requests are different, and allergies require separate attention. Ingredients in stocks, dressings, breads and desserts should be reviewed as carefully as the main dishes. If some guests are eating another menu, discuss how alternatives will be identified and served.

Choose dishes that suit the occasion. Small handheld bites can work well for a reception, while a seated meal may call for a more substantial centrepiece. A considered plant-based option belongs within the overall menu and service plan, with its own proper portion and presentation.
